newsitem.title: UK: Britain ready to contribute to Zaire mission.
newsitem.headline: Britain ready to contribute to Zaire mission.

text.p: Britain is ready to contribute troops to a humanitarian relief operation in Zaire but Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday vital details about the international mission still needed to be worked out.

"Ministers agreed the UK should be ready to contribute constructively to the international response, including to a multinational force, providing a satisfactory plan can be worked out," a statement from Major's office said.

The statement was released after a meeting of ministers at Major's official London home and ended a week of hesitation by Britain, once a major colonial power in Africa, about becoming involved in an area it believes is not its "back yard".

"We will contribute, we will definitely send troops," Major told reporters later. But he said how many troops Britain would send, what the scope of the mission would be and what its "exit strategy" would be were questions still to be answered.
Canada has offered to command the force to bring assistance to hundreds of thousands of refugees in Zaire.
"It is a complex and difficult situation on the ground," said the statement. "It is difficult terrain, there is no clear ceasefire and very little information is available."
Media reports have talked of Britain sending around 3,000 troops and the statement from Major's office stressed Britain would seek to maximise the safety of any British forces sent.
A meeting will take place in New York on Thursday bringing together all parties interested in aiding refugees fleeing fighting between Tutsi rebels and Zaire's army.

"We are discussing urgently with other potential contributors the scale and nature of the response," the statement said. President Bill Clinton has agreed in principle to order U.S. troops to take part in the relief force, the White House announced later.

Britain had said its thinking on whether to join the international mission would depend largely on the position taken by the United States. Major plans to speak to Clinton later on Wednesday, or early on Thursday.

Major said the British had decided to take part because of the heavy death toll among the hundreds of thousands of refugees in eastern Zaire. Soon 20,000 people would be dying every day and Britain could not stand aside, Major said.
"We believe that there should be an urgent response. We will be part of that urgent response," Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told reporters.
The statement said some measures would need to be taken immediately, such as an increase in food supplies to the accessible concentrations of refugees around Goma and Bukavu.
The longer term requirements would be to get emergency aid to the more inaccessible parts of eastern Zaire and to begin the repatriation of refugees.
